A mechanism-guided, low-input Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strategy for 
attenuating antibiotic resistomes under oxygen re-entry during 
anaerobic fermentation
Chaosheng Liao a,b
, Mingjie Zhang a, Wenlong Dai a, Xiaolong Tang a,b, Pan Wang a,  
Ning Mao a, Ping Li a,*
a College of Animal Science, Guizhou University, Guiyang, 550025, China
b Pratacultural College, Gansu Agricultural University, Lanzhou, 730070, Gansu, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Antibiotic resistance genes
Mobile genetic elements
Silage
Lactic acid bacteria
Aerobic exposure
Yeast
A B S T R A C T
Oxygen re-entry during the handling of anaerobically fermented biomass is accompanied by changes in microbial 
communities and antibiotic resistance profiles. This study evaluated the effects of different lactic acid bacterial 
inoculants on the attenuation of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in cattail silage during aerobic exposure after 
anaerobic fermentation. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, we tracked ARGs, mobile genetic elements 
(MGEs), and microbial succession in the control (CK), Levilactobacillus brevis (LB), a self-isolated Lactiplantibacillus 
plantarum (LP), and mixed-culture (M) treatments after 60 d of fermentation and 0–9 d of aerobic exposure. The 
resistome was dominated by glycopeptide- and tetracycline-resistance genes, with tetM and vanY as the major 
subtypes. Throughout the exposure period, LP maintained the lowest ARGs abundance, whereas LB enriched 
tetracycline resistance and the mixed culture did not provide additional ARGs attenuation. In all treatments, 
MGEs, mainly integrase- and plasmid-associated markers, covaried with ARGs, and their mobility potential 
gradually decreased during prolonged exposure. Aerobic exposure also induced clear microbial succession, 
including the disappearance of major ARGs hosts and the late enrichment of yeasts such as Pichia and Candida, 
which were negatively associated with ARGs abundance. Network analysis, random forest modeling, and partial 
least squares path modeling suggested that physicochemical changes induced by oxygen re-entry were linked to 
microbial community restructuring, accompanied by shifts in MGEs profiles and ARGs dynamics Overall, inoc­
ulation with the self-isolated LP strain, together with limiting aerobic exposure time, provides a practical and 
low-input strategy for reducing ARGs burden and potential mobility risk during the handling of fermented 
biomass.
1. Introduction
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as a major global threat 
to human and animal health, and its strong environmental dimension is 
now widely recognized within the One Health framework [1]. Antibiotic 
resistance genes (ARGs) and associated mobile genetic elements (MGEs) 
are increasingly viewed as environmental contaminants because they 
mediate horizontal gene transfer among pathogens, opportunistic 
pathogens and commensal microorganisms across clinical, agricultural 
and natural ecosystems [2,3]. Global syntheses show that ARGs are 
widespread in soils, waters and other environmental media, with agri­
cultural systems often exhibiting elevated ARGs loads relative to non- 
agricultural environments [4–6]. Manure production, storage and land 
application can further mobilise ARGs and MGEs, creating a continuum 
of AMR risk from farm to the wider environment [7,8].
Within ruminant production, forage resources are commonly pre­
served through solid-state anaerobic fermentation, particularly in re­
gions with harsh climates or short growing seasons [9,10]. During this 
anaerobic fermentation process, large amounts of plant biomass are 
compacted and stored under oxygen-limited conditions, where dense 
and dynamic microbial communities assemble and drive rapid physi­
cochemical changes (e.g., pH decline and organic acid accumulation). 
Importantly, oxygen re-introduction is often unavoidable during sub­
sequent handling and utilization, imposing a sharp redox perturbation

that can trigger community reassembly, organic acid consumption and 
substrate depletion. Recent work has reported diverse ARGs assem­
blages in fermented forage matrices and suggested that substrate type, 
anaerobic fermentation conditions, fermentation quality and manage­
ment practices can markedly influence ARGs occurrence and persistence 
[11,12]. Residual materials, leachates, and ARGs-carrying microbes 
entering manure handling chains may further facilitate dissemination to 
soils, waters and even plant surfaces, linking fermented forage systems 
to the feed–animal–environment continuum [13,14]. However, the 
successional dynamics of resistomes across the anaerobic fermenta­
tion–to–aerobic re-exposure transition, and their implications for envi­
ronmental AMR dissemination, remain insufficiently resolved under 
practical oxygen re-introduction scenarios.
Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) inoculants are widely used to improve 
anaerobic fermentation performance by accelerating lactic acid pro­
duction, lowering pH and inhibiting spoilage yeasts and moulds [15,16]. 
Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (L. plantarum) is among the most applied 
species because of its robust growth and acidification capacity across 
diverse forages. Beyond agronomic benefits, LAB inoculation has 
recently been shown to influence AMR-related risks in fermented forage 
and related matrices by altering the abundance of ARGs, MGEs and 
potential bacterial hosts [17,18]. At the same time, some LAB strains 
carry intrinsic or acquired resistance determinants and prophages, 
raising concerns about their possible contribution to ARGs dissemina­
tion in food and feed chains [19,20]. Moreover, indirect pathways 
mediated by acidification strength, organic acid profiles and oxygen 
availability may generate stage-dependent impacts on ARGs hosts and 
MGEs-linked transfer potential, which remain mechanistically unclear.
Cattail (Typha spp.) is an under-utilized wetland plant that has been 
explored as a low-cost forage resource in high-altitude or resource- 
limited pastoral regions [21]. Its high moisture content, fibrous struc­
ture and epiphytic microbiota can challenge stable and hygienic 
anaerobic fermentation, and the system can be vulnerable to aerobic 
deterioration, fungal proliferation and nutrient loss if management is 
suboptimal [9,22]. These features make cattail-derived fermented 
forage matrices a relevant model for interrogating resistome dynamics 
under comparatively high-risk conditions. Meanwhile, shotgun meta­
genomics combined with ecological network inference and multivariate 
causal modeling enables joint profiling of ARGs, MGEs and microbial 
communities and helps identify key physicochemical and biotic drivers 
shaping mobile resistomes in complex ecosystems [23,24].
Here, we established a controlled cattail plant-biomass anaerobic 
fermentation system with and without inoculation of a locally selected 
Lactiplantibacillus plantarum and monitored fermentation characteristics, 
physicochemical properties, bacterial and fungal communities, ARGs 
and MGEs across anaerobic fermentation and a subsequent aerobic re- 
exposure phase using shotgun metagenomics. Co-occurrence network 
analysis, random forest models and partial least squares path modeling 
were employed to identify environmental variables, microbial groups 
and MGEs associated with resistome dynamics and to unravel potential 
pathways linking LAB inoculation to changes in ARGs and MGEs as­
semblages. We hypothesised that LAB inoculation would mitigate 
resistome-related risks by strengthening acidification and modifying 
organic acid profiles, thereby suppressing potential ARGs-host bacteria 
and reducing MGEs-associated mobility potential, with additional 
regulation arising from fungal–bacterial niche replacement during pro­
longed aerobic re-exposure.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials preparation
Cattail samples were collected from the Hongyuan Experimental 
Base, affiliated with the Sichuan Academy of Grassland Sciences in 
Sichuan Province, China (32◦46′N, 102◦33′E, elevation 3500 m). The 
harvested cattail were shredded and chopped into 1–2 cm segments, 
then randomly allocated into four groups, each with three replicates. To 
reflect the routine use of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) inoculants in prac­
tical production and to compare the inoculation effects of LAB with 
different fermentation types, Levilactobacillus brevis(L. brevis), a hetero­
fermentative LAB, and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum(L. plantarum), a 
predominantly homofermentative LAB, were selected for inoculation. 
The treatments were as follows: (1) CK, equal amounts of sterile water 
required for activation of bacteria are included; (2) L. brevis (LB, 106 cfu/ 
g FM); (3) L. plantarum (LP, 106 cfu/g FM); and (4) LB + LP (M, 106 cfu/g 
FM). This comparative design was used to evaluate the effects of natural 
fermentation, single-strain inoculation, and mixed-strain inoculation 
strategies on fermentation characteristics, microbial succession, and 
ARGs dynamics in cattail silage during subsequent aerobic exposure. 
The CK group served as the uninoculated baseline for assessing natural 
fermentation and the natural succession of ARGs, whereas the LB, LP, 
and M groups were used to determine whether different LAB inoculation 
strategies produced distinct or complementary effects.
The inoculants used in this study included self-isolated L. brevis and 
L. plantarum strains. These strains were originally isolated from oat 
silage collected from the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau and were selected 
from a laboratory lactic acid bacterial strain collection based on their 
acid-producing ability and growth performance during preliminary 
screening. They were identified as L. brevis and L. plantarum based on 
partial 16S rDNA sequencing, sequence similarity analysis, and pre­
liminary physiological and biochemical characterization. Before appli­
cation, the strains were activated and diluted with sterile water to obtain 
the target viable cell concentration of 106 CFU/g fresh matter. The 
inoculant suspension was sprayed evenly onto the chopped cattail using 
a hand sprayer, and the same volume of sterile water was added to the 
CK treatment. Additional phenotypic and preliminary biochemical 
characteristics of the two inoculant strains are provided in Supplemen­
tary Table S1. After inoculation and thorough mixing, approximately 
2.0 kg of treated material was manually packed into polyethylene bags 
and vacuum-sealed for anaerobic fermentation for 60 days.
The aerobic exposure test followed the methodology described by 
[15]. In brief, the fermented cattail samples were placed in 1.0 L sterile 
plastic buckets, wrapped in two layers of coarse cotton fabric to reduce 
contamination and moisture loss, then kept at room temperature (25 
◦C). A thermocouple sensor was installed at the geometric center of the 
silage sample in each plastic container. These sensors were connected to 
an online 48-channel data logger (MDL-1048 A, Shanghai Tianhe 
Automation Instrumentation Co., Ltd., China), configured to record the 
temperature of each silage unit at 24-h intervals. Samples were collected 
at 3 d intervals during aerobic exposure, specifically on days 0, 3, 6, and 
9. Day 0 represented the initial state before aerobic exposure, whereas 
days 3 and 6 were used to reflect stage-specific changes during aerobic 
exposure. Since previous studies have observed clear deterioration- 
related changes after approximately 7 d of aerobic exposure [25], the 
endpoint was set at 9 d to ensure that a clear late-stage aerobic deteri­
oration state could be captured. A total of 48 samples (four inoculation 
treatments × four storage durations × three replicates) were included in 
the experimental design for subsequent analysis.
2.2. Sample composition analysis
A 10 g portion of each stored sample was homogenized with 90 mL of 
sterile water using a laboratory blender for 1 min, then filtered through 
four layers of gauze. The resulting filtrate was centrifuged at 4500 ×g for 
15 min at 4 ◦C. Concentrations of butyric, propionic, acetic, and lactic 
acids were quantified via high-performance liquid chromatography 
(HPLC) as described by [26]. Ammoniacal nitrogen levels were 
measured following the protocol established by [27]. The pH of each 
sample was determined using a pH meter (APERA pH 700, Shanghai 
San-Xin Instrumentation Co., Shanghai, China).
Approximately 200 g of each storage sample was oven-dried at 65 ◦C 
until a constant weight was achieved to assess dry matter (DM) content,

2.3. DNA extraction, metagenomic sequencing, and analysis of ARGs and 
MGEs
Genomic DNA from each sample was isolated using the CTAB 
extraction protocol. Subsequently, 1 μg of genomic DNA was randomly 
sheared into approximately 350 bp fragments using a Covaris ultra­
sonicator. Library construction included end repair, A-tailing, adaptor 
ligation, purification, and PCR amplification. Initial library quantifica­
tion was performed using a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer, after which the li­
brary was diluted to 2 ng/μL. Insert size was evaluated using an Agilent 
2100 Bioanalyzer. After confirming the expected insert size, the effec­
tive library concentration was quantified by qPCR, with a threshold of 
>3 nM used to validate library quality. Qualified libraries were pooled 
according to effective concentration and the intended sequencing data 
volume, followed by paired-end sequencing using the Illumina platform 
with a PE150 strategy.
Raw sequencing reads were preprocessed with Readfq (https://gith 
ub.com/cjfields/readfq) to generate high-quality clean reads for down­
stream analyses. The filtering criteria included: (a) removal of reads 
containing a high proportion of low-quality bases (quality score ≤38, 
default threshold 40 bp); (b) removal of reads with excessive ambiguous 
bases (N; default threshold 10 bp); and (c) removal of reads with adapter 
overlap exceeding 15 bp. RawData represented the original sequencing 
data generated for each metagenomic sample, whereas CleanData rep­
resented the effective sequencing data retained after quality filtering. 
Only CleanData were used for subsequent assembly, gene prediction, 
taxonomic annotation, and ARGs/MGEs analyses.
Clean reads were assembled using MEGAHIT with the meta-large 
preset. Assembled scaffolds containing ambiguous bases (N) were split 
at N positions to generate scaftigs without Ns. Assembly quality was 
evaluated based on scaftigs longer than 500 bp, including the number of 
assembled scaftigs, average length, N50, and N90. These parameters 
were used to assess the continuity and quality of the metagenomic as­
semblies before downstream annotation.
Open reading frames were predicted from scaftigs longer than 500 bp 
using MetaGeneMark with default parameters. Predicted genes shorter 
than 100 nt were removed. CD-HIT was then used to remove redundant 
genes and construct a non-redundant unigene catalog, with the 
following parameters: -c 0.95, −G 0, -aS 0.9, −g 1, and -d 0. CleanData 
from each sample were mapped back to the non-redundant unigene 
catalog using Bowtie2 with the parameters –end-to-end, −-sensitive, –I 
200, and -X 400. Genes with reads ≤2 in each sample were filtered out 
before downstream abundance analysis.
For abundance normalization, gene abundance was calculated based 
on the number of reads mapped to each unigene and the corresponding 
gene length. The normalized abundance of gene k was calculated as: Gk 
= (rk/Lk) / Σi(ri/Li). where Gk represents the normalized abundance of 
gene k, rk represents the number of reads mapped to gene k, and Lk 
represents the length of gene k. The normalized unigene abundance was 
then used to calculate taxonomic, ARGs, and MGEs relative abundances 
by summing the abundance of unigenes assigned to each corresponding 
category.
Unigene sequences were aligned against the NCBI NR database 
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) using DIAMOND BLASTp (https:// 
github.com/bbuchfink/diamond/) [31], with an E-value threshold of 
1 × 10–5. The analysis included Bacteria, Fungi, Archaea, and Viruses. 
For each sequence, alignments with E-values within 10 times the mini­
mum E-value were retained. Because a single sequence can have 
multiple alignments, the lowest common ancestor (LCA) algorithm, as 
implemented in MEGAN, was used for taxonomic assignment [32]. The 
relative abundance of each taxon was calculated by summing the 
normalized abundance of unigenes assigned to that taxon.
Unigenes were aligned against the CARD database (https://card. 
mcmaster.ca/) using the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI) tool pro­
vided by CARD. ARGs-like sequences were identified using the RGI built- 
in BLASTp algorithm with the default E-value threshold of <1 × 10–30. 
The relative abundance of each ARO, ARGs type, or ARGs subtype was 
calculated by integrating the normalized abundance of CARD-annotated 
unigenes assigned to the corresponding ARGs category [33–35].
For MGEs analysis, an ARGs-associated scaftig-based strategy was 
used. First, assembled scaftigs were compared with the CARD database 
to identify scaftigs carrying ARGs-like sequences. The corresponding 
ARGs-containing scaftigs were then extracted according to CARD 
annotation results and gene prediction files. These ARGs-containing 
scaftigs were further compared with MGEs databases, including Inte­
grall (version 2021.09), ISfinder (version 2023.10), and Plasmid 
(version 2021.06), to screen for integrase-, insertion sequence-, and 
plasmid-associated elements located on ARGs-associated scaftigs. 
BLASTn hits with sequence identity ≥90% and E-value ≤1 × 10–7 were 
retained as MGEs-like sequences. These thresholds were used to reduce 
weak or ambiguous matches and improve the stringency of MGEs 
annotation. The ARGs and MGEs mining results from scaftigs were 
summarized for downstream analyses of ARGs-associated mobility 
potential.
2.4. Statistical analysis
A general linear model (GLM) was employed using the default GLM 
procedure in SPSS software (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) to evaluate 
the individual and interactive effects of LAB inoculant treatment and 
aerobic exposure duration on the fermentation characteristics and 
chemical composition of cattail silage during aerobic exposure. Duncan's 
multiple range test was used for mean separation when significant ef­
fects were detected, and statistical significance was declared at P < 0.05. 
Multiple comparisons of ARGs and MGEs abundances among LAB 
inoculant treatments and aerobic exposure durations were performed 
separately using GraphPad Prism.
Co-occurrence network analysis was conducted to explore potential 
associations among ARGs, MGEs, and microbial taxa. Microbial taxa 
with detection frequencies below 60% and relative abundances below 
0.5% were removed before network construction. Spearman's correla­
tions were calculated among ARGs, MGEs, and retained microbial taxa, 
and P values were adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. 
Only strong and significant correlations with |R| > 0.8 and adjusted P <
0.05 were retained. Networks were constructed in R and visualized using 
Gephi version 0.10. Network relationships were interpreted as ecolog­
ical associations rather than direct evidence of host-resolved ARGs 
transfer.
Random forest modeling, Mantel tests, Procrustes analysis, and 
partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) were conducted in R. 
Random forest models were used to identify the major environmental, 
chemical, and microbial predictors of ARGs abundance. Model perfor­
mance was evaluated using the out-of-bag prediction procedure, and 
variable importance was quantified using the increase in mean squared 
error (%IncMSE). The stability of variable importance was assessed 
using bootstrap-derived standard errors and 95% confidence intervals, 
and Boruta analysis was applied to classify predictors as confirmed, 
tentative, or rejected variables.
Mantel tests and Procrustes analysis were performed using the vegan 
package to evaluate the relationships among ARGs profiles, MGEs pro­
files, microbial communities, and environmental variables. Bray–Curtis 
dissimilarity was used for ARGs profiles, MGEs profiles, and microbial 
communities, whereas Euclidean distance was used for standardized 
environmental and chemical variables. Mantel correlations were

PLS-PM was performed using the plspm package to evaluate putative 
association pathways linking environmental factors, chemical compo­

performance was evaluated based on path coefficients, R2 values of 
endogenous latent variables, and the global goodness-of-fit index. The 
robustness of the association-based conclusions was further evaluated 
by comparing the directional consistency among random forest 
modeling, Mantel tests, Procrustes analysis, co-occurrence network 
analysis, and PLS-PM. Therefore, the identified pathways and network 
relationships were interpreted as association-based ecological patterns 
rather than definitive causal relationships.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Succession of ARGs and MGEs under aerobic exposure
To contextualize resistome succession during aerobic exposure, we 
first characterized the fermentation microenvironment and substrate 
matrix of cattail silage. Across 0–9 d exposure, pH increased and 
ammonia-N accumulated at the late stage, while fermentation acids 
were progressively depleted, with the lowest lactic acid and acetic acid 
levels observed at mid-exposure (Table 1). In parallel, dry matter 
increased and structural carbohydrate fractions (NDF and ADF) became 
enriched, whereas WSC declined during mid-exposure (Table 2), 
consistent with substrate depletion and compositional concentration 
effects under oxygen ingress (Peng et al., 2018). Notably, LP established 
the strongest initial acidification and maintained lower ammonia-N, 
providing a distinct physicochemical niche that can shape microbial 
succession and downstream ARGs and MGEs dynamics. Against this 
physicochemical backdrop, we next characterized the dynamics of ARGs 
and MGEs across treatments and exposure duration.
A total of 23 ARGs types and 171 ARGs subtypes were identified 
across 48 silage samples (Fig. 1a and Table 3). Among these ARGs, 10 
types were consistently detected (100% of the ARGs types), with 
glycopeptide antibiotic and tetracycline antibiotic being the most 
abundant (Fig. 1a and Table 3). Glycopeptide antibiotic and tetracycline 
antibiotic evidently underpinned the variation in total ARGs abundance 
(Fig. 1b). Among the ARGs subtypes, tetM had the highest abundance, 
followed by the vanY gene in the vanG cluster and the vanY gene in the 
vanM cluster. Zhao et al. demonstrated that the distribution of ARGs is 
related to ARGs carried by different bacteria [36], and different lactic 
acid bacteria lead to changes in ARGs abundance during the silage 
process [18]. A similar phenomenon was observed in this study: ARGs 
distributions differed among treatments with various additives and 
shifted progressively with exposure duration (Fig. 1b). Overall, the 
reduction effect on ARGs was achieved by the 9th day of aerobic 
exposure. Surprisingly, the CK treatment exhibited a trend of increasing 
followed by decreasing total ARGs abundance, whereas LP treatment 
markedly reduced overall ARGs levels. This is consistent with the 
observation by reference Zhang et al. that LP additives reduced ARGs in 
alfalfa silage [12]. Exogenous lactic acid bacterial additives frequently 
harbor a small number of ARGs [20], contributing to elevated ARGs risks 
in silage feed. LB treatment possibly contained tetracycline ARGs, 
enhancing tetracycline antibiotic abundance (Fig. 1b) and consequently 
raising its overall abundance. Mixed additives often lead to competition 
among bacterial strains, affecting the microbial community [37]. This is 
the fundamental reason for the changes in ARGs under the M treatment. 
Variations in ARGs abundance in the M treatment suggest that the mixed 
additives in this study failed to eliminate ARGs.

The dissemination of ARGs is closely related to MGEs. To assess their 
transmission risk, we annotated three major MGEs (Fig. 2). Across all 
treatments, the variations in MGEs were predominantly influenced by 
Integrase and Plasmid, which represented the majority share. Thus, 
Integrase and Plasmid emerge as the principal contributors to the overall 
dynamics of MGEs. Moreover, during aerobic exposure, changes in 
MGEs across all treatments exhibited a synchronous trend with ARGs 
abundance, further highlighting the critical role of MGEs in driving

antagonistic effects. This is probably because competition among mi­

with increasing exposure days. MGEs are also carried by microbes, and 
these changes are consistent with our previous discussion on microbial 
competition and the influence of environmental conditions on microbial 
dynamics. Specifically, single-strain treatments were significantly more 
effective than multi-strain treatments, and environmental changes had a 
notable impact on the succession patterns of MGEs.
3.2. Microbial community succession during aerobic exposure
Microbes act as carriers of ARGs, and their succession indicates 
changes in ARGs. Annotating microbial communities helps to analyze 
ARGs risk (Fig. 3). During all aerobic exposures, Bacillota and Pseudo­
monadota were dominant. As aerobic exposure increased, the relative 
abundance of Bacillota gradually decreased, a result attributed to the 
proliferation of aerobic bacteria limiting Bacillota activity [43] Bacillota 
are major producers of ARGs, responsible for carrying and disseminating 
ARGs [44]. The changes in Bacillota were consistent with the changes in 
ARGs, explaining the observed reduction in ARGs in this study. More­
over, Pseudomonadota comprises many aerobic pathogens, including 
Enterobacteriaceae, potential hosts for ARGs [45]. Aerobic conditions 
promoted the rise of Pseudomonadota, resulting in increased ARGs in CK 
treatment between days 3–6. Overall, the duration of aerobic exposure 
influenced the silage bacterial community, and the succession of Bacil­
lota and Pseudomonadota significantly impacted ARGs. Notably, Asco­
mycota showed high abundance in the late stages of aerobic exposure, 
suggesting that it may influence the silage environment and determine 
the fate of ARGs during fermentation. Ascomycota is often recognized as 
a key fungal group for breaking down lactic acid in silage (e.g., yeast). 
Some yeasts utilize lactic acid as a substrate [46], which may explain 
their increase relative to the initial lactic acid (Table 1). Traditionally, the 
low pH environment caused by high lactic acid inhibits the proliferation 
of most Pseudomonadota, including undesirable Enterobacteriaceae in 
silage [16]. At day 0, the lowest pH in the LP treatment inhibited the 
growth of most potential ARGs hosts (Table 1), resulting in the lowest 
ARGs abundance. However, excessive lactic acid supported the prolif­
eration of Ascomycota in LP. Further investigation is needed to determine 
if Ascomycota amplification involves potential ARGs carriers and its 
specific role in ARGs dissemination risks. Therefore, analysis of microbial 
communities at the host species level will help reveal the potential roles 
and mechanisms of Ascomycota in ARGs dissemination risks.
At the species level, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum (L. plantarum) and 
Levilactobacillus brevis (L. brevis) are the dominant lactic acid bacteria 
during fermentation, with their high abundance closely linked to lactic 
acid production and maintenance of a low pH environment, significantly 
inhibiting the growth of potential pathogens (e.g., Escherichia coli) and 
reducing ARGs dissemination risk [47]. However, the potential role of L. 
brevis as a host of Tetracycline ARGs cannot be overlooked. The changes 
in L. brevis under M and LB treatments were consistent with changes in 
Tetracycline relative abundance, supporting our earlier hypothesis. 
Roberts and Schwarz reviewed the distribution of resistance genes, 
including Tetracycline, among agricultural and environmental bacteria, 
clearly highlighting the widespread presence of tetM, tetO, and other 
Tetracycline resistance genes in lactic acid bacteria such as L. brevis, 
emphasizing their potential role as a resistance gene reservoir [48]. 
Evidently, when considering its use as a silage fermentation promoter, 
the potential risk of ARGs dissemination from L. brevis must be thor­
oughly evaluated. On the other hand, in the later stages of aerobic 
exposure, the abundance of yeasts such as Pichia membranifaciens, Pichia 
kudriavzevii, and Candida californica increased significantly. These yeasts 
may indirectly regulate microbial community structure by metabolizing 
lactic acid, altering environmental pH and chemical composition [49]. 
This regulatory effect might suppress the proliferation of Bacillota bac­
teria, the primary carriers of ARGs (Fig. 3a), ultimately reducing ARGs 
abundance and dissemination risk. Furthermore, Li et al. highlighted in 
composting studies that microbial consortia, including yeasts, signifi­
cantly enhanced ARGs removal rates by raising compost temperatures, 
accelerating water loss, and promoting nitrogen (ammoniacal nitrogen) 
fixation [50]. Similarly, Cao et al. found that microbial compost in­
oculants with yeasts reduced ARGs abundance, and this reduction 
correlated with a decrease in Bacillota abundance [51]. Although yeast 
proliferation might limit the growth of ARGs hosts, explaining the 
reduction in ARGs abundance during LP treatment and late aerobic 
exposure, further studies are needed to determine whether they harbor 
potential ARGs carriers. Moreover, the specific mechanisms of yeast 
involvement in ARGs dissemination risks remain unclear, and their po­
tential role in horizontal gene transfer needs to be explored further.

established a stronger acidified environment and reduced ammonia-N

stronger acidification and reduced protein degradation. Because 
acidification-matched controls were not included and L. plantarum 
strains with different acidification capacities were not compared in this 
study, it remains difficult to fully separate the strain-specific effect of LP 
from fermentation-quality-driven effects. Future studies should incor­
porate acidification-matched controls and multiple L. plantarum strains 
with contrasting acidification capacities to further distinguish strain- 
specific effects from fermentation-quality-driven effects.
3.4. Contributions of MGEs, microbes, and silage environment to ARGs 
dissemination in aerobic exposure of cattail silage
This study explored the relationships between ARGs, microbial 
communities, MGEs, and environmental factors using Procrustes 
analysis and Mantel tests (Fig. 5). The results showed a significant cor­
relation between the spatial distribution of ARGs and MGEs (M2 = 0.33, 
P = 0.001), indicating that MGEs may play an important role in ARGs 
mobility potential. Moreover, ARGs exhibited a strong association with 
microbial communities (M2 = 0.41, P = 0.001), suggesting a possible 
link between bacterial population changes and ARGs dissemination 
potential. Nonetheless, Mantel test analysis also revealed a strong cor­
relation between ARGs and microbial communities (R = 0.833, P =
0.001), indicating that ARGs variation was not solely related to MGEs- 
associated mobility but may also be influenced by microbial commu­
nity structure. Furthermore, environmental factors also played a sig­
nificant role in ARGs variation (R = 0.289, P = 0.001). They may 
indirectly influence MGEs-associated mobility potential through selec­
tion pressure, thereby affecting ARGs dynamics. In conclusion, the evi­
dence from this study suggests that MGEs may contribute importantly to 
ARGs dissemination potential, while microbial community structure and 
environmental factors also play regulatory roles. However, because 
direct transfer events and host-resolved ARGs and MGEs linkages were 
not experimentally validated, these findings should be interpreted as 
ecological associations and mechanistic indications rather than defini­
tive evidence that horizontal gene transfer was the dominant route.
To determine the impact of environmental and microbial factors on 
ARGs during aerobic exposure, random partial dependence plots were 
constructed using randomForest, rfUtilities, rfPermute, and tidyverse 
packages to quantify the response of key environmental factors and 
microbes to ARGs dissemination (Fig. 6a, b). The results showed that 
ARGs were primarily influenced by microbes such as L. brevis, L. plan­
tarum, and Pichia membranifaciens. This aligns with our earlier inference 
that different lactic acid bacteria inoculants and the increased yeast 
during exposure are the primary microbial drivers of ARGs dissemina­
tion. Regarding environmental factors, DM, NDF, acetic acid, pH, tem­
perature and ADF were dominant. Environmental factors significantly 
influenced the distribution and abundance of ARGs by regulating mi­
crobial com Specifically, moisture content (DM), temperature, acidic 
conditions (acetic acid, pH), and substrate availability (fiber) acted on 
potential ARGs host bacteria, driving the dynamic changes in ARGs 
[8,24,50,55]. Consequently, the partial least squares path model (PLS- 
PM) highlighted the direct and indirect impacts of environmental fac­
tors (temperature, acetic acid, pH), chemical components (DM, NDF, 
ADF), and key microbial communities (top 5 in importance) on ARGs 
variations (Fig. 6c). The results showed that environmental factors 
indirectly drove ARGs changes by directly regulating microbial com­
munities (λ = 0.378, P < 0.05). Moreover, microbial communities not 
only directly influenced ARGs abundance (λ = 0.429, P < 0.01) but also 
significantly affected MGEs profiles (λ = 0.731, P < 0.01), further 
influencing ARGs dissemination potential. Chemical composition has no 
direct effect on ARGs (P > 0.05) but primarily influences the spread of 
ARGs by regulating microbial communities (λ = 0.418, P < 0.01).
The PLS-PM model further highlighted the important role of MGEs in 
ARGs variation (λ = 0.484, P < 0.01). This result indicates that, within 
complex microbial communities, ARGs dynamics are closely related to 
MGEs profiles, which may be jointly influenced by environmental and 
chemical factors. However, this regulation occurs primarily indirectly 
through microbial mediation, as neither environmental nor chemical

[56]. Notably, the effects of environmental and chemical factors on 
ARGs largely depend on changes in microbial community structure, 
while the microbial regulation of ARGs is mainly mediated by MGEs.

significantly decreased, thereby lowering the potential risk of ARGs 
transfer (Fig. 7a). These changes reflected a complex microbial response 
to aerobic stress, in which oxygen exposure induced both taxonomic and 
functional restructuring of the silage microbiome. Such shifts in com­

Similar bacterial–fungal niche differentiation has been documented in 
the decomposition of plant-derived organic matter, where fungal pro­

and competing for carbon resources [58,59]. In this study, such niche 
expansion and resource-driven microbial competition jointly reshaped 
community composition and reduced the ecological potential for ARGs 
dissemination during the later stages of aerobic exposure.
Acetic acid acts as an organic acid to lower pH and synergistically 
regulates horizontal ARGs transfer efficiency along with temperature. 
On the other hand, as a substrate utilized by certain bacteria [60], acetic 
acid regulates ARGs dissemination risks through competitive in­
teractions. However, while serving as a bacterial substrate, acetic acid's 
antimicrobial properties also inhibit the activity of some yeasts [61]. 
This inhibitory effect led to growth fatigue in yeast-like fungi in the 
other three treatment (CK, LB and M) groups (Fig. 3, Table 1), resulting 
in high ARGs abundance. In the LP, although low levels of acetic acid 
were detected, its significant inhibitory effect on ARGs remained 
evident. LP significantly inhibited ARGs-carrying bacteria by promoting 
the proliferation of lactic acid bacteria. Particularly under aerobic 
exposure, LP fermentation produced to high levels of lactic acid, serving 
as a primary energy source for yeast-like fungi, promoting their prolif­
eration and ecological niche occupation, further restricting the growth 
and proliferation of ARGs-carrying bacteria.
Overall, the key novelty of this study is that ARGs attenuation during 
aerobic exposure was linked not only to reduced MGEs-mediated 
mobility and suppression of bacterial hosts, but also to bacter­
ial–fungal niche replacement driven by the expansion of yeast-like fungi. 
Specifically, our results reveal that microbial community dynamics in­
fluence ARGs dissemination during aerobic exposure of silage, and that 
yeast-like fungi may inhibit ARGs-carrying bacteria through competi­
tion for substrate resources and ecological niche occupation. This 
finding extends previous studies that mainly focused on bacterial hosts 
and MGEs by highlighting the potential role of fungal succession in 
regulating resistome dynamics during aerobic exposure. Future in­
vestigations should further clarify whether these yeasts directly carry 
ARGs or indirectly suppress ARGs by reshaping bacterial niches, sub­
strate competition, and organic acid metabolism. These findings also 
suggest that future silage inoculant development should consider not 
only fermentation quality, but also ARGs-host suppression, MGEs ac­
tivity, bacterial–fungal interactions, and resistome safety during aerobic 
handling.
4. Conclusion
Reduction of ARGs-related risks during aerobic exposure was linked 
to the coordinated effects of acidified microenvironments, host com­
munity restructuring, and reduced MGEs-associated mobility potential. 
Notably, the self-isolated LP inoculant outperformed other inoculation 
schemes in reducing the abundance of potential ARGs-hosting bacteria 
and lowering ARGs mobility-related risk. From a bioprocess perspective, 
targeted single-strain inoculation can be deployed to enhance bio­
resource safety during the most practical exposure stage in silage use. 
The present study provides an association-based framework for inte­
grating microbial process control with antimicrobial resistance risk 
management in high-altitude forage systems.
